# Retrieval and Document Intelligence {#sec-retrieval-practice}

In production, retrieval is an evidence service with two jobs. It publishes
trustworthy representations of source material, and it returns only the
evidence a caller is allowed to see. The theory in @sec-rag-retrieval explains
retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), while @sec-context-engineering explains
how selected evidence becomes model input; this chapter turns both into an
operable system. The work produces a **retrieval release**: a versioned corpus,
a tested query path, and the evidence needed to deploy or roll it back
[@lewis2020rag].

Building a release starts from a contract, written before any product
comparison. The contract records the **corpus boundary**, the query classes the
system must answer, the **success evidence** required for release, and the
authority under which each source may be used. It also sets freshness and
deletion service levels, latency and cost budgets, and a rollback window.
Without these facts, a fast index or a high benchmark score has no operational
meaning.

| Contract field | Question the release must answer |
|---|---|
| Corpus boundary | Which repositories, formats, languages, dates, and source revisions are in scope? |
| Query classes | Which lookups, paraphrases, tables, temporal questions, and no-answer cases matter? |
| Success evidence | Which parse, retrieval, citation, answer, security, latency, and cost tests must pass? |
| Authority | Which principal, tenant, purpose, policy, and retention rule govern each item? |
| Change | What are the freshness SLA and deletion SLA, and where are they measured? |
| Recovery | Which last-known-good release remains available, and how is rollback exercised? |

@fig-retrieval-pipeline separates offline publication from the authorized
online path. Evaluation observes every stage on both paths, from source
revisions to the cited answer.

## Preserve evidence lineage

A document file can carry several views of the same content. A PDF can contain
a digital text layer, page images, annotations, fonts, form fields, tags, and
hidden content; these views can disagree [@iso2020pdf]. The pipeline therefore
stores the original **source object** and its content digest before deriving
anything, and every changed byte sequence receives a new **source revision**. A
renderer then creates a rendition; a parser produces a document element; a
segmenter splits elements into chunks, the text units the index stores, each
with a chunk ID and exact source span; an embedding model maps each chunk to a
vector in one declared space; and an index snapshot publishes the vectors. This
provenance chain must remain resolvable from a returned citation
[@w3c2013prov].

```{dot}
//| label: fig-document-lineage
//| fig-cap: "Each derived retrieval object remains bound to an immutable source revision."
digraph {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  graph [nodesep=0.18, ranksep=0.25];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1",
        penwidth=1.0, margin="0.12,0.08"];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.65];
  S [label="Source object\nrevision + digest"];
  R [label="Rendition\npage + coordinates"];
  D [label="Document element\nkind + reading order"];
  C [label="Chunk ID\nsource span + parent"];
  V [label="Embedding\nmodel + space"];
  I [label="Index snapshot\ngeneration + watermark"];
  E [label="Evidence ID\nclaim locator"];
  S -> R -> D -> C -> V -> I -> E;
}
```

A useful lineage record includes the source identifier, revision and digest;
media type and acquisition time; tenant, access-control policy, rights, and
retention state; renderer, parser, schema, normalizer, and segmenter revisions;
page coordinates and reading order; raw and normalized text; parent element and
heading path; and every published index generation, an immutable, versioned
build of the index. Raw evidence is stored separately from normalized search
text, so normalization can change without rewriting history.

### Ingestion is a publication protocol

Ingestion runs as a release pipeline in seven stages:

1. **Acquire and authorize.** Resolve the source identity, bytes, rights,
   tenant, retention rule, and current access-control state.
2. **Inspect.** Verify media type independently of the filename; scan for
   malware; enforce byte, page, pixel, archive, and execution limits. Reject or
   quarantine malformed, encrypted, active, or suspicious input.
3. **Normalize and render.** Preserve the original, then create deterministic
   renditions with explicit page boxes, rotation, coordinate origin, and units.
4. **Parse.** Read the digital text layer where reliable; otherwise apply OCR,
   layout analysis, table and equation recognition, and reading-order recovery.
5. **Extract and validate.** Produce document elements and structured extraction
   with evidence selectors, pointers to the source spans that support each
   value. Retain uncertainty rather than inventing values.
6. **Segment and embed.** Create retrieval units within authorization and
   retention boundaries; reject silent truncation at model input limits.
7. **Stage, reconcile, and publish.** Check counts, hashes, omissions,
   tombstones, and coverage. Atomically publish a complete generation or keep
   the previous one. Partial output is never quietly promoted.

Retries must be idempotent. A worker crash on page 17, a duplicate delivery, or
the same URI returning changed bytes must produce a reconciled revision, not a
half-old, half-new index.

## Measure document understanding

An @gls-ocr engine recognizes text from pixels. A @gls-vlm reads page images
and text together. Neither
term includes every document task: detecting layout, restoring reading order,
reconstructing a table, recognizing an equation, and mapping coordinates are
separate operations. Born-digital text extraction is separate again. A toolkit
such as Docling can compose several of these operations, while an end-to-end
model may emit a structured representation directly [@auer2024docling].

Parser quality varies with the kind of document, so the choice of parser rests
on a local evaluation. That evaluation uses a held-out corpus, documents kept
out of every tuning decision, divided by **document stratum**. A stratum is a
group of documents that can fail in a materially different way from the rest:
born-digital and scanned pages, multiple scripts, right-to-left text,
rotations, low resolution, multiple columns, forms, tables, equations,
handwriting, redactions, hidden text, and malformed files. OmniDocBench is
useful background, but its public average cannot replace this per-stratum
evaluation [@ouyang2025omnidocbench].

Transcription quality is reported as character error rate (CER):

$$
\mathrm{CER}=\frac{S_c+D_c+I_c}{N_c},
$$

where $S_c$, $D_c$, and $I_c$ count character substitutions, deletions, and
insertions, and $N_c$ is the number of characters in the reference. CER
measures transcription only. Element detection precision/recall, reading-order
error, table structure similarity, formula recognition, field-level
precision/recall, and provenance-locator accuracy are measured separately.
Low-confidence, high-impact cases go to human review, and the review rate is
recorded as its own figure rather than hidden in a single score.

### Structured extraction has two kinds of validity

JSON Schema can prove that output has the permitted shape and types, but it
cannot prove semantic correctness. A schema-valid invoice can still carry the
wrong total. Each field therefore keeps an evidence selector and an explicit
`unknown` state, and the extractor is allowed to abstain when evidence is
missing or ambiguous. Domain postconditions such as subtotal arithmetic, date
ranges, identifier checksums, and cross-field consistency check the extracted
values. Automatic retries must not turn uncertainty into fabricated certainty.

### Visual retrieval is an evaluated alternative

Retrieval can also work on page images directly. ColPali-style visual
retrieval embeds each page image as many vectors and matches a query against
them by late interaction, which combines the per-vector matches at query time
[@faysse2024colpali]. It can retain layout signals lost by text conversion and
can work well for visually rich or multilingual documents. It also changes the
cost, storage, accessibility, explainability, and generator requirements.

The comparison runs text retrieval, visual retrieval, and a multimodal
combination on the same labeled queries. Even a path that skips most parsing
still needs stable page identity, authorization, provenance, accessible text or
an equivalent accommodation, and structured extraction when a downstream system
needs fields rather than pixels.

## Segment for retrieval and citation

The **retrieval unit** is what ranking returns; the **citation unit** is the
smallest source region a reader can verify. They need not be identical. A
retriever may score a proposition or passage, then expand to its parent element
or section for context. Every unit should retain a stable chunk ID, parent
element, source revision and source span, heading path, language, page and
coordinates, content digest, policy, and valid-time interval.

As @sec-rag-retrieval explains, the right chunk size depends on the corpus and
its queries. Segmentation strategies are therefore compared on the same query
set: structure-aware elements, fixed windows, sentences, propositions, and
parent-child expansion. The boundary and overlap policy is versioned. Overlap
can protect boundary evidence, but it also increases index size and creates
duplicate results; context assembly must detect duplicates without discarding
useful corroboration. A chunk must never cross an authorization or retention
boundary.

## Authorize the online query

The **query contract** contains the query, a verified principal and tenant,
validated metadata filters, an as-of time, result and context budgets, ranking
policy, and resolved index generation. Access control is an eligibility
condition, applied before any relevance scoring. The system must authorize
before candidate generation, using current resource state; post-filtering a
global top-k can leak data and underfill the authorized result, returning fewer
authorized items than requested.

For query $q$, subject $s$, evaluation time $t$, and immutable generation $g$,
define the authorized universe

$$
\begin{gathered}
U(q,s,t,g)=\\
\{c\in I_g\mid\\
P(s,\mathrm{read},c,t)=\mathrm{allow},\\
c.\mathrm{valid\_from}\le t<c.\mathrm{valid\_to},\\
\neg c.\mathrm{tombstone}\}.
\end{gathered}
$$

Here $I_g$ is index generation $g$, $c$ is a candidate, and $P$ is the policy
decision for subject $s$ at time $t$. Retrieval returns top-k only from $U$.
Missing or invalid policy metadata fails closed. The wrong tenant must never
appear in candidates, reranker input, debug output, traces, or caches; this is
the retrieval analog of @sec-security-authorization.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-retrieval-query
//| fig-cap: "The query path builds candidates only from the authorized universe and records every later decision."

  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  graph [nodesep=0.18, ranksep=0.28];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,

        penwidth=1.0, margin="0.12,0.08"];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.65];
  Q [label="Query + principal\npolicy + generation"];
  U [label="Authorized universe"];
  CS [label="Sparse\ncandidates"];
  CD [label="Dense\ncandidates"];
  CV [label="Visual\ncandidates"];
  F [label="Fusion"];
  R [label="Rerank + context budget"];
  E [label="Evidence record + citations"];
  { rank=same; CS; CD; CV; }
  Q -> U;
  U -> CS; U -> CD; U -> CV;
  CS -> F; CD -> F; CV -> F;
  F -> R -> E;
}
```

## Choose representations by measured behavior

The four retrieval families defined in @sec-rag-retrieval make different
operational trade-offs:

- **Sparse retrieval** such as BM25 is a strong lexical baseline for names,
  identifiers, and rare terms. Its analyzer, language rules, field weights, and
  parameters are part of the index version.
- **Dense retrieval** uses a dual encoder, so document representations can be
  precomputed offline while the query is encoded online. Learned similarity can
  connect paraphrases and can also blur decisive lexical distinctions
  [@karpukhin2020dpr].
- **Late interaction** keeps token-level document representations and combines
  their matches at query time. ColBERT uses it for first-stage retrieval as well
  as for reranking [@khattab2020colbert].
- A **cross-encoder** scores each query-document pair jointly. It is often more
  expensive and is normally applied to a bounded candidate union. It cannot
  recover evidence that candidate generation omitted.

The relative order of these families changes from dataset to dataset. BEIR and
MTEB are useful for method comparison and model screening, while the release
decision rests on results for the local query strata
[@thakur2021beir; @muennighoff2023mteb]. The lexical baseline comes first.
Each additional representation and reranker is then measured as an ablation, a
run with and without that one component.

### Freeze the embedding compatibility contract

An embedding is a model-specific representation whose similarity reflects its
training objective. The compatibility record therefore names the model and
tokenizer digest, embedding dimension, normalization, distance metric, query
prefix and document prefix (fixed strings some models expect before each
input), truncation rule, and input limit. Cosine similarity, inner product, and
Euclidean distance are interchangeable only when their normalization
assumptions make them so.

Query and document vectors must name the same embedding-space revision, and the
system rejects dimension, prefix, normalization, or space mismatches. A model
change normally requires a new generation and a re-embed migration, which
recomputes every stored vector with the new model. Equal dimensions or similar
model names do not establish compatibility. Query encoding and index selection
switch together in one atomic routing change, even when models are served
through the gateway described in @sec-serving-stack.

### Fuse ranked lists by position

Sparse, dense, and visual scores are usually not calibrated to one another.
Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), introduced in @sec-rag-retrieval, combines ranks
instead [@cormack2009rrf]. The form used here adds a weight for each list. For
the set of ranked lists $\mathcal{L}$, define

$$
s_{\mathrm{rrf}}(d)=
\sum_{L_j\in\mathcal{L}:d\in L_j}\frac{w_j}{k_0+r_j(d)},
$$

where $d$ is a candidate, $L_j$ is ranked list $j$, $r_j(d)$ is its one-based
rank in that list, $w_j\ge0$ is the list weight, and $k_0>0$ is the fusion
constant. A candidate not returned by a list contributes zero. RRF does not
calibrate relevance scores or use their magnitude. Candidate depth, weights,
the fusion constant, missing-item behavior, and deterministic tie-breaking are
ranking-policy settings, tuned on validation data (labeled queries set aside
for tuning) and frozen before holdout evaluation.

This small implementation makes those semantics testable:

```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists, k0, weights=None):
    """Return (document, score) pairs in deterministic descending order."""
    if k0 <= 0:
        raise ValueError("k0 must be positive")
    weights = weights or [1.0] * len(ranked_lists)
    if len(weights) != len(ranked_lists):
        raise ValueError("one weight is required for each ranked list")

    scores = {}
    for weight, ranked in zip(weights, ranked_lists):
        if weight < 0:
            raise ValueError("weights must be non-negative")
        for rank, document_id in enumerate(dict.fromkeys(ranked), start=1):
            scores[document_id] = scores.get(document_id, 0.0) + weight / (k0 + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
```

Reranking and context selection remain separate decisions. Candidate depth,
rerank depth, final top-k, and the context budget are each measured
independently, and the reranker runs within its own latency budget and input
limit. Diversity controls such as maximum marginal relevance can reduce
redundant context, but they trade relevance against diversity and do not
guarantee deduplication.

## Publish an index generation

A vector index supplies exact or approximate neighbor search. A production
store must additionally meet the **index contract**, which covers durability,
metadata, filters, consistency, backup, recovery, tenant isolation, and
migration. Each generation records:

- corpus watermark and source coverage;
- metadata schema, policy fields, and filter selectivity distribution;
- analyzer, embedding space, distance, and ranking-policy revisions;
- vector count, dimension, hashes, tombstones, and duplicate policy;
- index algorithm and parameters, build hardware, duration, and recovery time;
- exact-search baseline, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) recall, latency
  percentiles, concurrency, and cost;
- supported update, delete, backup, restore, and rollback behavior.

HNSW is a graph-based approximate-neighbor design whose memory, build, recall,
and latency trade-offs depend on the workload [@malkov2018hnsw]. DiskANN-style
designs use SSD-aware graph search to change that resource balance
[@subramanya2019diskann]. The choice of store rests on measurement under the
local workload. The comparison covers exact scan, HNSW, DiskANN, inverted-file
(IVF) indexes, or compression variants under realistic filters, updates,
concurrency, cache state, and tenant skew, and it reports ANN recall against
the exact eligible top-k at each important filter selectivity.

A release manifest can be small and still prevent accidental mixing:

```yaml
generation: corpus-2026-08-07-03
source_watermark: "2026-08-07T08:00:00Z"
parser: doc-parser@sha256:...
segmenter: headings-v4
embedding_space: embed-model-v7-d1024-cosine
ranking_policy: hybrid-rrf-rerank-v5
policy_schema: acl-v3
deletion_watermark: "2026-08-07T08:05:00Z"
```

A new immutable generation is built as a **shadow index**, which runs
alongside the serving index without answering users. The shadow is backfilled,
its source counts, digests, and tombstones are reconciled, and it catches up on
changes to an explicit watermark. Shadow queries run first; dual reads against
the old and new generations then compare quality, authorization, freshness,
latency, and cost by query class. One atomic routing change moves both the
query encoder and the index, and the last-known-good generation stays available
through the rollback window. A vector from an incompatible new embedding space
is never used to search an old index.

### Freshness and deletion cover every copy

The freshness SLA runs from a committed source change to an eligible result,
and the deletion SLA from revocation to absence. A deletion creates a tombstone
that propagates to the vector index, lexical index, reranker and answer cache,
published snapshot, replicas, and every in-flight migration generation. Logical
suppression must happen promptly; physical erasure follows the declared
retention process. Cache keys include tenant, policy version, generation, and
as-of time. A stale result is explicit and never silently broadened as fallback.

The test suite covers insert, update, ACL change, source deletion, interrupted
backfill, duplicate replay, partial index failure, corrupt snapshot, and
rollback. It must show that a deleted document cannot reappear from a cache,
old snapshot, or shadow index.

## Return an evidence bundle

The retrieval response is an evidence bundle. Each item carries an immutable
evidence ID; source object, source revision, digest, span or page coordinates;
index and ranking revisions; stage-specific ranks; applied policy and time;
and truncation, underfill, timeout, stale-result, and fallback flags. Scores of
different kinds stay separate in the bundle rather than being merged into one
calibrated probability.

Every material claim in an answer is bound to one or more retrieved evidence
IDs. Evaluation measures citation precision, citation recall, locator validity,
entailment or contradiction (whether the cited evidence implies the claim or
conflicts with it), and answer correctness [@gao2023citations];
@sec-rag-retrieval defines the two citation metrics. A generated citation that
was not present in the evidence bundle is invalid. Rendering a saved answer
reauthorizes its evidence, because a once-valid source may have been revoked.

### Retrieved documents are untrusted

Text, metadata, OCR output, image text, and annotations are untrusted data as
defined in @sec-rag-retrieval: material an answer may draw on, which carries no
authority. An indirect prompt injection, an instruction planted in a retrieved
page, therefore remains page content [@greshake2023indirect]. It cannot grant
authority, become a tool instruction, change the tenant, disable citations, or
request data exfiltration. The runtime keeps instructions and evidence in
distinct channels, allow-lists tool actions, validates arguments, and applies
authorization again at each side effect.

The test suite also covers a poisoned corpus, in which an attacker may insert
apparently relevant chunks to steer answers or citations [@poisonedrag2025].
Defending against it means restricting ingestion authority, recording source
trust and provenance, reviewing unusual source or ranking changes, and
retaining a known-clean rollback generation. Content scanners catch some attacks; the protection that does not
depend on detection is that retrieved text has no authority of its own.

## Evaluate layers and failure modes

One end-to-end score cannot identify where evidence was lost. Each layer
therefore has an oracle, the reference output that layer should produce, and
the deployed stage is compared with it. @sec-rag-retrieval defines the
retrieval metrics in the table (Recall@k, nDCG@k, and MRR).

| Layer | Evidence for release |
|---|---|
| Parse quality | CER, element detection, reading order, table structure, formula and field-level accuracy, provenance validity |
| Candidate retrieval | Recall@k, nDCG@k, MRR, filtered recall, exact-search comparison, underfill rate |
| Fusion and rerank | Candidate recall before rerank, nDCG after rerank, truncation, diversity, deterministic fallback |
| Context and answer | Answer correctness, faithfulness, citation precision/recall, contradiction, abstention calibration |
| System | Zero unauthorized exposure, freshness/deletion SLA, p95 latency, availability, and cost per accepted answer |

The evaluation splits by document family rather than placing sibling chunks at
random in train and test. The query set includes exact identifiers,
paraphrases, negation, multilingual questions, tables, temporal questions,
ambiguous entities, multi-hop evidence, hard negatives (non-relevant passages
that closely resemble relevant ones), and no-answer cases. Model judges, models
used to grade answers, are calibrated against a stable human-reviewed sample.
Frameworks such as RAGAs can help automate measurement; the product threshold
comes from the release contract [@es2024ragas].

The acceptance suite needs negative cases: wrong tenant, deleted document,
stale revision, poisoned chunk, malformed table, empty retrieval, duplicate
chunk, selective-filter underfill, reranker timeout, index failure, and
no-answer behavior. Fallback and rollback are exercised for each relevant
failure. An outage may reduce ranking quality under a named policy; it may
never weaken authorization or fabricate evidence.

## Operate the release lifecycle

1. **Freeze the contract.** Record corpus, query classes, policy, service levels,
   metrics, thresholds, latency and cost budgets, and rollback criteria.
2. **Build a labeled corpus.** Stratify documents, queries, relevance judgments,
   citations, security cases, and expected abstentions.
3. **Establish a lexical baseline.** It exposes corpus and judgment failures
   before embedding and ANN complexity arrive.
4. **Evaluate candidates.** Compare parsing, segmentation, sparse, dense,
   visual, fusion, reranking, and context policies as controlled ablations.
5. **Build and reconcile.** Publish only a complete immutable generation with a
   manifest, provenance, policy, and tombstone coverage.
6. **Shadow.** Replay production-shaped queries without serving the result.
7. **Canary.** Route a small authorized cohort and monitor quality, leakage,
   freshness, latency, cost, and fallbacks.
8. **Promote or roll back.** Switch atomically; keep and exercise the
   last-known-good generation.
9. **Monitor drift.** Sample queries and documents by stratum, investigate
   changes, and preserve decision traces without logging sensitive payloads by
   default.
10. **Requalify.** A parser, segmenter, embedding space, analyzer, index,
    reranker, policy schema, corpus boundary, or material workload change is a
    requalification trigger.

The output is a retrieval release record: the immutable manifest, evaluation
results, security and failure evidence, freshness and deletion measurements,
canary decision, owner, approval, rollback target, and requalification
triggers. That record is the handoff to the generator or agent team and the
input to the wider evaluation practice in @sec-eval-practice.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

Each lower layer constrains every layer above it. Missing evidence cannot be
recovered by a reranker, unauthorized evidence cannot be made safe by a prompt,
and an incompatible index cannot be repaired by gateway routing. Agents in
@sec-agents-practice multiply retrieval calls, so quality, authorization,
latency, and cost must hold per call and over the complete task. The full system
wiring appears in @sec-wiring-stack.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The contested decision

Teams often debate products before they have a representative corpus or an
exact-search baseline. The corpus and the baseline come first, because every
product is measured against them. A store, parser, embedding model, or
reranker is acceptable only when its complete release record meets the local
contract. There is no defensible universal chunk size, candidate depth, fusion
constant, vector count threshold, or product default.
:::
